---
title: "Explore ratings, plans and score probabilities"
description: "Three reproducible ggplot2 examples, with interactive Plotly views and the values behind each figure."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.8, dev.args = list(bg = "white"))
```

**Who scores more strictly? What changes when we add tasks? Which scores does
our model predict?** Explore each question below, then adapt the code to your
own assessment. These examples require the **unreleased 0.2.4 candidate**;
follow the [installation instructions](../index.html#install-the-version-used-here).
All observations here are synthetic.

Hover or tap to inspect values, drag to zoom and double-click to reset.
Click a legend entry to hide or show its series. Each section also provides a
static ggplot and a table, so the results remain readable without interaction.

## Start with familiar R tools

Install `ggplot2`, `plotly` and `htmlwidgets` if needed. These are optional for
mfrmr's base graphics. The sequence is the same for the supported views:

```r
saved_plot <- plot(result, draw = FALSE)
figure <- as_ggplot(saved_plot)           # Customize with ggplot2
interactive_figure <- plotly::ggplotly(figure)
```

`plot()` computes the requested plot data. The conversion steps redraw those
saved values; they do not refit the model or create new confidence intervals.
The [visual guide](../articles/mfrmr-visual-diagnostics.html) identifies supported
conversions. Check custom geoms, facets, labels and interval layers after
conversion; an arbitrary ggplot is not guaranteed to look identical in Plotly.

```{r libraries}
library(mfrmr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

# Apply a style to these figures without changing the session's global theme.
gallery_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#E6EBF1"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#24334B"),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "#394B63"),
    legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(12, 18, 12, 12))
```

## 1. See rater differences, together with uncertainty

Load the same ratings as the README: 48 people, six raters and three criteria.
Each row is one observed rating; 1 denotes lower and 4 higher performance in
this illustrative rubric. Missing ratings are absent rows, not zeros.

```{r measurement}
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_operational")
fit <- fit_mfrm(ratings, person = "Person", facets = c("Rater", "Criterion"),
  score = "Score", rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4,
  category_policy = "preserve", method = "MML", model = "RSM")
diagnostics <- diagnose_mfrm(fit, residual_pca = "none")
rater_plot <- plot(fit, type = "rater_severity", diagnostics = diagnostics,
  facet = "Rater", draw = FALSE)
rater_values <- plot_data(rater_plot, "data")
rater_gg <- as_ggplot(rater_plot) + gallery_theme +
  labs(x = "Rater severity (logits)", y = NULL)
```

**Read the horizontal position first.** Higher rater locations mean lower
expected scores for the same person and criterion. The horizontal segments are
95% model-based normal intervals, using this fit's observed-information SEs.
Zero is the centering reference. A location is not a verdict on rater quality,
and overlap of two intervals is not a formal pairwise test.

```{r rater-interactive, fig.height=4.4}
rater_hover <- rater_gg + aes(text = sprintf(
  "Rater: %s<br>Severity: %.2f logits<br>95%% interval: [%.2f, %.2f]<br>Use: %s",
  Level, Estimate, CI_Lower, CI_Upper, CIUse))
rater_widget <- ggplotly(rater_hover, tooltip = "text", height = 420)
rater_widget <- layout(rater_widget, dragmode = "zoom")
rater_widget
```

<details>
<summary>Static ggplot and exact values</summary>

```{r rater-static, fig.alt="Six rater severity estimates with 95 percent model-based normal intervals. R01 is near minus 0.61 and R06 near plus 0.41 logits. Higher locations mean stricter scoring; zero is a centering reference."}
rater_gg
```

```{r rater-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(rater_values[c("Level", "Estimate", "CI_Lower", "CI_Upper", "CIUse")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Rater", "Logits", "95% lower", "95% upper", "Interval use"))
```

</details>

R01 and R06 are about `r round(rater_values$Estimate[rater_values$Level == "R01"], 2)`
and `r round(rater_values$Estimate[rater_values$Level == "R06"], 2)` logits here.
For your data, inspect `CIEligible`, `IntervalStatus` and `CIUse`; unavailable
bounds must remain unavailable. Keep the assumptions in
`plot_data(rater_plot, "notes")` with the figure. See the
[rater-interval guide](../articles/mfrmr-facet-intervals.html) for other interval targets.

## 2. Compare tasks and raters before collecting more ratings

This is a separate **observed-score** planning example. The bundled G-study
contains 40 persons crossed with eight raters and six tasks. Content and
Organization are continuous synthetic score components. We report their
prespecified, equally weighted mean and generalize over tasks and raters.
These scores and their variances are not MFRM logits.

```{r planning}
data("mfrmr_example_gtheory_crossed", package = "mfrmr")
g_study <- mfrm_g_study(mfrmr_example_gtheory_crossed,
  scores = c("Content", "Organization"), person = "Person",
  rater = "Rater", task = "Task")
plans <- expand.grid(Raters = 1:4, Tasks = 1:6)
d_study <- mfrm_d_study(g_study, design_grid = plans,
  weights = c(Content = .5, Organization = .5))
plan_plot <- plot(d_study, metric = "Phi", x_var = "Tasks", draw = FALSE)
plan_values <- plot_data(plan_plot, "series")
plan_gg <- as_ggplot(plan_plot) + gallery_theme +
  labs(x = "Tasks per person", y = "Dependability of absolute score levels (Phi)")
```

**Follow one line to see the effect of more tasks at a fixed rater count.**
Phi concerns absolute score levels; it is not the probability of a correct
pass/fail decision. These are point projections for future complete balanced
plans. They omit variance-component estimation uncertainty and do not establish
that a plan is adequate for a particular decision. No universal cutoff is drawn.

```{r planning-interactive}
plan_hover <- plan_gg + aes(text = sprintf(
  "Tasks: %d<br>Raters: %d<br>Ratings per person: %d<br>Phi: %.3f<br>Status: %s",
  Tasks, Raters, Tasks * Raters, Value, Status))
plan_widget <- ggplotly(plan_hover, tooltip = "text", height = 470)
plan_widget
```

<details>
<summary>Static ggplot and plans with the same rating count</summary>

```{r planning-static, fig.alt="Four curves show projected Phi for one through six tasks with one, two, three or four raters. All use the equally weighted Content and Organization composite. These are point projections without uncertainty intervals."}
plan_gg
```

```{r equal-rating-plans, echo=FALSE}
equal_effort <- plan_values[plan_values$Tasks * plan_values$Raters == 12,
  c("Tasks", "Raters", "Value", "AbsoluteSEM", "Status")]
knitr::kable(equal_effort, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Tasks", "Raters", "Phi", "Absolute SEM", "Status"))
```

</details>

The table compares 2 × 6, 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 designs, each with twelve ratings per
person. Equal rating counts need not mean equal cost or participant burden.
For intervals and paired comparisons of plans, continue with the
[G/D-study tutorial](../articles/mfrmr-gtheory.html#compare-feasible-assessment-plans).

## 3. Explore what a rubric score means in the model

Return to the ordinal RSM fit from section 1. At each person location, the four
curves show the predicted probabilities of scores 1–4. This is the saved
**zero-additive-facet reference profile**: rater and criterion effects are held
at zero. It does not average across the people and raters in the observed data.

```{r probabilities}
curve_plot <- plot(fit, type = "ccc", draw = FALSE)
curve_values <- plot_data(curve_plot, "probabilities")
curve_gg <- as_ggplot(curve_plot) + gallery_theme +
  labs(x = "Person location (logits)", y = "Probability of the coded score")
# This example has four categories in one common RSM curve group.
stopifnot(length(unique(curve_values$CurveGroup)) == 1L)
categories <- unique(as.character(curve_values$Category))
```

**Move along the horizontal axis and compare all four curves.** A score with a
higher probability is still not a certain outcome. The curves are model point
predictions, not confidence bands or evidence that the rubric measures the
intended construct. Hiding a category does not renormalize the remaining
probabilities.

```{r probabilities-interactive}
curve_hover <- curve_gg + aes(text = sprintf(
  "Score: %s<br>Person location: %.2f logits<br>Probability: %.3f",
  Category, Theta, Probability))
curve_widget <- ggplotly(curve_hover, tooltip = "text", height = 450)
# Keep readable score labels if conversion appends internal group numbers.
for (i in seq_along(categories)) {
  curve_widget <- style(curve_widget, name = categories[i],
    legendgroup = categories[i], traces = i)
}
curve_widget
```

<details>
<summary>Static ggplot and probabilities at the reference person location</summary>

```{r probabilities-static, fig.alt="Four category probability curves across person locations. Score 1 predominates at low locations and score 4 at high locations. Probabilities sum to one at each location for the zero-additive-facet RSM reference profile."}
curve_gg
```

```{r probabilities-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(curve_values[abs(curve_values$Theta) < 1e-10,
  c("Category", "Probability", "CurveBasis")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Score", "Probability at zero", "Reference profile"))
```

</details>

Always state the coding direction: a higher score for *ease of understanding*
means something different from a higher score for *difficulty understanding*.
The model follows your coded scores; it cannot infer the intended direction.

## Keep the figure, values and interpretation together

Use `ggsave()` for the static ggplot and `saveWidget()` for a browser-readable
interactive HTML file. No Plotly account or running R server is needed for these
views. A shared HTML file includes its plotted data; use suitable identifiers
and remember that filtering or hiding a trace does not remove those data.

Run these commands in a folder where you want to keep the outputs.
Self-contained HTML export requires Pandoc. With `selfcontained = FALSE`, keep
the accompanying assets directory together with the HTML file.

```r
ggsave("rater-severity.png", rater_gg, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(rater_widget, "rater-severity.html", selfcontained = TRUE)
write.csv(plot_data(rater_plot, "data", format = "long",
  value_cols = c("Estimate", "CI_Lower", "CI_Upper")),
  "rater-severity-long.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(source = rater_plot, figure = rater_gg, widget = rater_widget,
  notes = plot_data(rater_plot, "notes")), "rater-severity.rds")
```

The saved mfrmr plot retains the interval definitions and diagnostics.
`ggplotly()` returns a Plotly widget, not an mfrmr result; keep its source plot
and notes alongside it. Use `plot_data_components()` to inspect available tables
and `plot_data(..., format = "long", value_cols = ...)` to build your own views.
For a raincloud of observed scores, use the original rating rows: estimates and
interval endpoints are different quantities. Hovering, zooming and legend filtering change the display, not the fitted
model or analysis population. New model fitting in a browser would require a
separately hosted R application.
